surfaces.title: Jezero Crater, Mars
surfaces.description: A real 360 degree photo of Jezero Crater on Mars, taken by NASA's Perseverance rover. The sky above and the ground below the photographed band are filled in. Drag to look all the way around.
surfaces.creditNote: Taken by the Perseverance rover on its third day on Mars (Feb 21, 2021). The sky above and the dark ground below are filled in.
surfaces.orbitHint: Hi, I'm Orbit! Drag to look around. Then tap the glowing dots!

hotspots.label: Far away hills
hotspots.title: The edge of Jezero Crater
hotspots.text: Those far-away hills are the rim of Jezero Crater. Long ago, rivers poured into this crater and made a lake. That was more than 3.5 billion years ago!

hotspots.label: Red ground
hotspots.title: Why is Mars red?
hotspots.text: The dirt on Mars has iron in it. The iron rusts, a bit like an old bike left in the rain. That is why the ground looks red.

hotspots.label: The sky
hotspots.title: A dusty sky
hotspots.text: Mars has thin air with lots of dust floating in it. To our eyes, the sky would look hazy and red, not blue like on Earth.

hotspots.label: The rover
hotspots.title: Meet Perseverance
hotspots.text: This is Perseverance, a robot explorer on Mars. It is looking for signs of ancient life. It also collects pieces of rock to study.

hotspots.label: About this picture
hotspots.title: A picture made of 142 photos
hotspots.text: This 360 degree picture is made of 142 photos. Perseverance took them on its third day on Mars. People on Earth joined them together.

surfaces.title: Earth from the Space Station
surfaces.description: A real NASA astronaut photo of Earth taken from the International Space Station, seen through a window: a green aurora over a cloudy ocean, with dark space and stars below. Drag to look a little around.
surfaces.credit: Image courtesy of the Earth Science and Remote Sensing Unit, NASA Johnson Space Center
surfaces.creditNote: Photo iss073e0247726 (eol.jsc.nasa.gov), June 12, 2025. The window frame is drawn.
surfaces.orbitHint: Hi, I'm Orbit! Look out of the window. Then tap the glowing dots!

hotspots.label: Green aurora
hotspots.title: The southern lights
hotspots.text: This green glow is an aurora, also called the southern lights. Tiny charged bits from the Sun, called the solar wind, make Earth's air glow. Green comes from oxygen.

hotspots.label: Glowing edge of Earth
hotspots.title: Earth's blanket of air
hotspots.text: This glowing edge is Earth's air, seen from the side. It is mostly nitrogen and oxygen, so we can breathe. It also shields us from much of the harmful radiation from the Sun.

hotspots.label: Clouds over the ocean
hotspots.title: Clouds over the ocean
hotspots.text: These clouds are floating over the Indian Ocean. Earth's oceans cover about 71 percent of the planet. Most of our planet is covered in water!

hotspots.label: Solar array
hotspots.title: A piece of the space station
hotspots.text: This orange grid looks like one of the station's big solar arrays. The station has 8 main solar arrays, and together they give it power.

hotspots.label: Space station speed
hotspots.title: A very fast trip
hotspots.text: The space station travels five miles every second. It goes all the way around Earth about every 90 minutes. The crew sees 16 sunrises and 16 sunsets each day!

hotspots.label: About this picture
hotspots.title: About this picture
hotspots.text: An astronaut took this photo from the space station on June 12, 2025. The station was 269 miles above the Indian Ocean, between Australia and Antarctica.

surfaces.title: Flying past the Moon
surfaces.description: A real NASA photo of the Moon, taken on the Artemis II mission from the Orion spacecraft, seen through a drawn cockpit window. It shows the side of the Moon we always see from Earth. Drag to look a little around.
surfaces.creditNote: Taken on the Artemis II mission (April 4, 2026): photo art002e009057, "The Nearside of the Moon". Cropped to the Moon. The cockpit window is drawn.
surfaces.orbitHint: Hi, I'm Orbit! We're flying past the Moon. Tap the glowing dots to explore!

hotspots.label: Dark gray patches
hotspots.title: The Moon's dark seas
hotspots.text: The dark patches are called maria, which means seas. But there is no water there! They are old lava that filled giant holes in the Moon long ago.

hotspots.label: Bright crater with rays
hotspots.title: Tycho Crater
hotspots.text: That bright spot with white streaks is Tycho Crater. It is more than 52 miles wide. It is young for a crater: about 108 million years old!

hotspots.label: Dark spot at the edge
hotspots.title: Orientale, a giant crater
hotspots.text: This dark spot at the edge is Orientale basin. It is a crater nearly 600 miles wide! Part of it is on the far side of the Moon, which we never see from Earth.

surfaces.title: Flying past Jupiter
surfaces.description: A real NASA photo of Jupiter, made from 27 pictures taken by the Cassini spacecraft as it flew past in December 2000, seen through a drawn cockpit window. Jupiter has no solid ground. Drag to look up and down.
surfaces.creditNote: A true colour picture made from 27 photos taken by Cassini on December 29, 2000: PIA04866, "Cassini Jupiter Portrait". The cockpit window is drawn.
surfaces.orbitHint: Hi, I'm Orbit! Jupiter has no ground to land on, so we fly past. Tap the glowing dots!

hotspots.label: Big reddish oval
hotspots.title: The Great Red Spot
hotspots.text: This reddish oval is the Great Red Spot. It is a giant storm bigger than Earth! It has been swirling for hundreds of years.

hotspots.label: Orange and white stripes
hotspots.title: Stripes made of clouds
hotspots.text: Jupiter's stripes are clouds. The dark orange stripes are called belts, and the light ones are called zones. Strong winds push them east and west in opposite directions.

hotspots.label: Small white ovals
hotspots.title: White oval storms
hotspots.text: These small white ovals are storms too. Even the smallest storms in this picture are about as big as the biggest hurricanes on Earth!
